writtenQuestions.answer: MP3 (MPEG Audio Layer III). Also acceptable: WAV, MIDI, WMA, AAC, FLAC, OGG.

writtenQuestions.q: Outline TWO advantages of using a serif font.
writtenQuestions.answer: First, serif fonts improve readability in print at small sizes because the small strokes (serifs) at the ends of letterforms help guide the reader's eye along the line of text, making it easier to track and distinguish individual characters quickly. Second, serif fonts convey a sense of authority, tradition and professionalism, making them well-suited to formal documents, newspapers, books and corporate communications where credibility is important.

bandDescriptors.full: 2/2 — States TWO distinct advantages with explanation: (1) the serifs guide the eye along the line of text, improving readability in print at small sizes; AND (2) conveys professionalism, authority or tradition, making them well-suited to formal documents.
bandDescriptors.partial: 1/2 — States one clear advantage with explanation, but the second advantage is absent, vague, or repeats the same idea differently.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 0/2 — States only 'they look professional' with no explanation, or names one advantage with no reasoning.

writtenQuestions.q: Describe the differences between vector and bitmapped images.
writtenQuestions.answer:
Bitmap (raster) images are made up of a fixed grid of individual pixels, each assigned a specific colour value. This means they are resolution-dependent — if a bitmap image is enlarged beyond its original size, individual pixels become visible, causing the image to appear blurry or "pixelated" and losing quality.

Vector images, by contrast, are defined by mathematical equations that describe shapes, lines, curves and colours rather than pixels. This makes them resolution-independent — a vector image can be scaled to any size without any loss of quality, always remaining perfectly sharp and smooth.

Bitmap images are better suited to complex photographic content with subtle colour gradations, while vector images are preferred for logos, icons and illustrations that need to be reproduced at multiple sizes.

bandDescriptors.full: 3/3 — Correctly defines bitmap (fixed pixel grid, resolution-dependent, becomes pixelated/blurry when enlarged) AND vector (mathematical equations defining shapes, resolution-independent, scales to any size without quality loss). Identifies which type suits different use cases (photos vs logos/icons).
bandDescriptors.partial: 2/3 — Defines both types but the reason why one is resolution-dependent and the other is not is missing or inaccurate. Use cases may be omitted.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1/3 — Describes only one image type, or describes both but without explaining what makes each technically distinct.

writtenQuestions.q: Explain how a director could use different camera shots in the multimedia production process. Use examples to support your answer.
writtenQuestions.answer:
A director uses a variety of camera shots strategically to guide the audience's attention, convey meaning and create emotional impact throughout the production.

Wide shots (establishing shots) are used at the beginning of a scene to show the environment and situate the audience within the setting — for example, a sweeping wide shot of a city skyline establishes location and scale. Close-up shots focus tightly on a character's face or a significant object to convey intense emotion or draw attention to important details, such as a close-up of trembling hands to suggest fear or anxiety. Medium shots show a character from the waist up and are commonly used for dialogue scenes to capture both expression and body language simultaneously.

Low-angle shots — where the camera points upward at a subject — are used to make a character appear powerful, threatening or authoritative, such as filming a villain from below. High-angle shots do the opposite, making subjects appear small, vulnerable or powerless.

Tracking shots follow a subject as they move, maintaining engagement and creating a sense of dynamic action. Together, these different shot types form the visual language of the production and work in combination to create effective visual storytelling.

bandDescriptors.full: 4/4 — Explains at least three different shot types (e.g. wide/establishing, close-up, medium, low-angle, high-angle, tracking) with an explanation of the purpose or emotional effect of each, and at least one specific example demonstrating how a director would use it.
bandDescriptors.partial: 2–3/4 — Identifies multiple shot types but the explanation of their purpose is incomplete for some, or examples are absent or too generic.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1/4 — Names shot types with no explanation of their effect or purpose, or describes only one shot type with an example.

writtenQuestions.q: Explain the process of using special effects in multimedia production. Use examples to support your answer.
writtenQuestions.answer:
The use of special effects (SFX and VFX) in multimedia production involves a structured process across pre-production, production and post-production stages.

In pre-production, the director and VFX supervisor collaborate on a detailed storyboard that identifies every scene requiring special effects. Technical requirements are assessed — including the software (e.g., Adobe After Effects, Autodesk Maya), hardware specifications and skill sets needed. Budgets and timelines for each effect are established at this stage.

During production, practical techniques are prepared. For live-action sequences requiring digital backgrounds or creatures, green screens are erected on set for chroma keying. Actors interact with markers or physical props that will later be replaced by CGI elements. Precise lighting, camera angles and coordination between the director and VFX team ensure the captured footage will integrate seamlessly with digital elements.

In post-production, digital assets — including 3D models, textures, particle effects and digital environments — are created or sourced and composited into the footage. New effect layers are added frame by frame and blended with the live-action material to achieve realism. For example, computer-generated imagery (CGI) is used in Marvel films to create photorealistic creatures, robots and large-scale destruction that would be physically impossible or prohibitively dangerous to film practically. Final colour grading, lighting adjustments and rendering complete the integration, producing a seamless final product.

bandDescriptors.full: 5/5 — Describes the process across all three stages: pre-production (storyboard, software/hardware planning, budget), production (green screen/chroma key setup, actor coordination with VFX markers), and post-production (compositing digital assets, CGI integration, colour grading, rendering). Uses at least one specific example (e.g. Marvel CGI creatures).
bandDescriptors.partial: 3–4/5 — Covers two of the three production stages in reasonable detail, or covers all three but one stage is significantly underdeveloped. May focus entirely on post-production.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1–2/5 — Describes special effects only as 'adding CGI in editing' without explaining the production pipeline stages or the planning and on-set work involved.

writtenQuestions.q: Why would a PNG file format be used instead of a JPEG file format?
writtenQuestions.answer: PNG (Portable Network Graphics) would be used instead of JPEG for two key reasons. First, PNG uses lossless compression — all original image data is preserved exactly and image quality is not compromised during compression, unlike JPEG which permanently discards data using lossy compression. Second, PNG supports transparent backgrounds, which is essential for web design and graphic work where images need to be layered over different backgrounds without a visible rectangular border. PNG is therefore preferred for logos, icons, graphics and any image requiring exact colour fidelity or transparency.

bandDescriptors.full: 2/2 — Identifies TWO reasons to choose PNG over JPEG: (1) lossless compression preserves full image quality with no data discarded; AND (2) PNG supports transparent backgrounds, making it suitable for layering over different backgrounds.
bandDescriptors.partial: 1/2 — States one correct reason with explanation but the second reason is absent or vague.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 0/2 — States only 'PNG is better quality' without explaining lossless compression, or confuses PNG and JPEG characteristics.

writtenQuestions.q: The home page of a website includes a banner image that needs to be adjusted to match the site's overall colour scheme and style guide. Outline steps to manipulate the banner image to ensure that it aligns with the website design.
writtenQuestions.answer: To align the banner image with the website's colour scheme and style guide: (1) Open the image in image editing software (e.g. Photoshop, GIMP). (2) Adjust the hue, saturation and colour balance to match the site's palette — for example, shifting dominant colours to align with the brand's primary and secondary colours. (3) Apply contrast and brightness adjustments to ensure text placed over the banner remains legible. (4) Ensure the banner is the correct aspect ratio and dimensions for the website layout (e.g. 1920×400px for a full-width header). (5) Optimise the image for fast loading by exporting at an appropriate file size and format (e.g. JPEG for photographs, PNG for graphics with transparency). (6) Test the banner across different screen sizes to confirm responsiveness and visual consistency with the overall design.

writtenQuestions.q: How do analogue and digital video types differ?
writtenQuestions.answer: Analogue video uses continuous signals — a smooth, uninterrupted variation in electrical voltage — to represent video information. This produces natural, smooth transitions but is susceptible to quality degradation over time and through copying. Digital video uses discrete signals represented as binary data (0s and 1s). Digital formats allow for higher and more consistent quality, easier editing and post-production processing, error correction, and lossless copying without generational quality loss. Digital video can also be compressed more efficiently and distributed via the internet, making it far more practical for modern production and distribution.

bandDescriptors.full: 2/2 — Correctly explains that analogue uses continuous electrical signals (smooth but degrades over time and through copying) while digital uses discrete binary data (consistent quality, easy editing, lossless copying, efficient compression for distribution).

writtenQuestions.q: Explain the potential advantages of using motion capture technology in a short, animated film.
writtenQuestions.answer:
Motion capture (MoCap) technology offers several significant advantages for a short animated film.

First, MoCap produces highly realistic and fluid character movements by recording the actual physical motion of human performers. This level of naturalism — including subtle weight shifts, micro-expressions and secondary motion — is extremely difficult to replicate through manual keyframing, resulting in more convincing, expressive characters.

Second, MoCap significantly improves production efficiency. Recording a performer's movement in real time captures complex animation data that would otherwise take animators weeks of manual work to create, reducing labour costs and production time.

Third, captured MoCap data is reusable across multiple projects or scenes. The same movement library can be applied to different characters, providing long-term value and consistency across a production.

Finally, for complex action sequences or crowd scenes in a short film, MoCap makes technically demanding animation achievable within a smaller budget, balancing quality and cost-effectiveness and making the final product more engaging and marketable.

bandDescriptors.full: 4/4 — Explains at least three distinct advantages with reasoning: (1) produces highly realistic, fluid movement including subtle expressions — difficult to replicate by manual keyframing; (2) production efficiency — captures complex animation data far faster than manual methods; (3) MoCap data is reusable across multiple scenes or characters; (4) makes technically demanding sequences achievable within smaller budgets.
bandDescriptors.partial: 2–3/4 — Identifies multiple advantages but explanations are brief or some overlap (e.g. 'realistic' and 'natural movement' treated as separate points when they are the same idea).
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1/4 — States only one advantage without elaboration, or identifies a benefit that applies equally to any animation technique rather than being specific to motion capture.

writtenQuestions.q: Describe the ethical implications of image manipulation and enhancement.
writtenQuestions.answer:
Image manipulation and enhancement in the multimedia industry raise significant ethical concerns across several areas.

Authenticity and misinformation are primary concerns. Heavily manipulated images — particularly in journalism and social media — can mislead the public by distorting facts or fabricating events. Altered images used in news reporting erode public trust and undermine the integrity of information. For example, digitally placing a person at a location they never visited can have serious legal and reputational consequences.

Beauty standards and mental health represent another major ethical issue. Over-editing of photographs in advertising and social media — removing blemishes, reshaping bodies or altering skin tone — creates unrealistic and unattainable beauty ideals that negatively impact viewers' self-perception and mental health, particularly among young people.

Privacy is also a concern. Manipulating images of real individuals without their consent — including using their likeness in contexts they did not agree to — violates privacy rights and can constitute defamation or harassment.

Copyright and ownership issues arise when manipulating images without proper attribution or when using another creator's work as the basis for manipulation without permission.

On the positive side, ethical image enhancement exists — for example, pixelating or blurring the faces of victims or children in traumatic news images to protect their privacy and dignity.

Ethical image manipulation should balance creative expression with honesty and transparency, particularly in advertising and journalism where audiences expect authenticity.

bandDescriptors.full: 5/5 — Identifies and explains at least four distinct ethical concerns: authenticity/misinformation (journalism, fabricating events), beauty standards and mental health (advertising, unrealistic ideals for young people), privacy and consent (using individuals' likenesses without permission), and copyright/ownership. Notes that some image enhancement is ethical (e.g. blurring victims' faces to protect privacy).
bandDescriptors.partial: 3–4/5 — Addresses three concerns with reasonable depth, or four concerns but one or more lacks explanation of why it is an ethical problem.
bandDescriptors.minimal: 1–2/5 — Focuses only on one concern (typically 'making images look fake') or lists concerns without explaining the ethical dimension of each.
